prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Ice, entire cakes of it. Crows feed on sand. So poor is this season the ground steals color from the tree-shadows. • Can it be that nothing is as far as here? Just look! How much past we have to cover this evening– • Come to think of it don't forget to pick off this self and that self along the way. Though that’s not right– you spit them out like pits. • If there is a partition between the outer and inner worlds, how is it that some water in me churns between the mountain ranges? How is it we are absorbed so easily by the ground— • Long nights for simple words. • Slant rhyme of current thinking and past thinking. A chewed over hour, late. Where the long ago past and the future come to settle scores. • Traveling and traveling, but so much interior unpicked over by the eyes. • Nothing is as far as here.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker depicts a bleak, impoverished season where even the landscape seems drained of life and color.
- The poem explores the feeling that the present place or moment is strangely distant, as if “nothing is as far as here.”
- The speaker reflects on shedding past selves during the journey, treating identity as something discarded along the way.
- The boundary between inner and outer worlds is questioned through images of water, mountains, and absorption into the ground.
- The poem connects travel through physical space with unresolved interior exploration, where past and future confront each other.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores alienation, memory, and the blurred boundary between inner and outer worlds through stark, surreal natural imagery and reflective fragments. It suggests that the most distant and difficult terrain is the self, making inner reckoning as vast and significant as any physical journey.

Keywords: Ice, Crows, Can

outputs.L2: Frozen slabs everywhere, whole masses of ice. Ravens pick at the sand for food. The season is so barren that the earth seems to drain the color out of the trees’ shadows. • Is it possible that no place lies farther away than this one? Look—there is so much of the past we must cross before night is over. • And while we are thinking of it, remember to strip away this version of the self and then that one as we go. No, that is not quite it—you discard them from your mouth the way you would stones from fruit. • If a wall separates the world outside from the world within, why does some water inside me surge among mountain ridges? Why do we sink into the earth so readily— • Simple words require very long nights. • The thoughts of now half-rhyme with the thoughts from before. A late hour, already gnawed and reconsidered. outputs.L3:
The poem presents a bleak and impoverished season in which the surrounding world appears drained of vitality. The landscape is not merely cold or bare; it seems almost emptied of color, warmth, and abundance. This atmosphere of deprivation shapes the speaker’s perception, making the external world feel like a reflection of emotional exhaustion. Nature itself appears diminished, as though the season has stripped away not only growth but also certainty, comfort, and meaning.

Within this desolate setting, the poem explores a strange sense of distance from the present moment. The idea that “nothing is as far as here” suggests that the speaker experiences the current place not as immediate or familiar, but as remote and difficult to grasp. “Here” becomes paradoxical: it is the point at which the speaker physically exists, yet it feels farther away than any remembered or imagined place. This creates a feeling of dislocation, as if the speaker is separated from the present by memory, longing, or inner estrangement.

The journey described in the poem also becomes a process of shedding former versions of the self. As the speaker moves through space, identity is treated as something unstable, something that can be left behind like worn-out clothing or discarded baggage. Past selves are not fully preserved; they are abandoned along the way, suggesting that travel involves loss as much as movement. The speaker’s identity is therefore not fixed, but made up of what has been carried, relinquished, and forgotten.

At the same time, the poem questions the boundary between the inner world and the outer landscape. Images of water, mountains, and absorption into the ground blur the distinction between body, mind, and environment. The landscape seems to enter the speaker, while the speaker also imagines dissolving into the landscape. This mutual absorption suggests that emotional states cannot be separated from the physical world; the terrain becomes a way of expressing inward experience, while the self becomes vulnerable to being overtaken by what surrounds it.

Ultimately, the poem connects travel through physical space with a deeper, unresolved interior journey. Movement across the landscape does not lead to simple progress or clarity. Instead, it brings the speaker into contact with conflicting pressures of past and future. The past remains present in the selves that have been shed, while the future remains uncertain and perhaps unreachable. The poem’s journey is therefore both geographical and psychological: it traces the speaker’s passage through a stark external world while also revealing an unfinished exploration of memory, identity, and becoming.
outputs.L4:
The landscape appears at first to be empty: a field hardened by frost, a black line of trees, a sky so pale it seems less like weather than like an absence of thought. Yet nothing here is truly empty. Every stone, every branch, every pool of dark water seems charged with a secret pressure, as if the outer world has been shaped by something inward and unresolved. Nature does not offer comfort; it becomes a mirror, severe and strange, reflecting states of mind that cannot be spoken directly.

The speaker moves through this terrain as though crossing both a physical place and a remembered one. Images rise in fragments: a bird suspended in cold air, a road vanishing into mist, the sound of water beneath ice, the sudden brightness of snow against darkness. These details do not simply describe a setting. They suggest a consciousness trying to locate itself among broken impressions, half-memories, and feelings that remain just beyond understanding. The natural world becomes surreal because memory itself is unstable. What is seen outside seems to belong equally to the mind; what is felt inside seems to take on the shape of the surrounding earth.

Alienation runs through the text as a quiet but persistent force. The speaker appears separated from others, from the familiar world, and even from the self. There is no easy homecoming, no clear destination, no simple division between past and present. Instead, the text unfolds in reflective fragments, as if thought can only proceed by flashes. Each image opens briefly, then withdraws. The result is a sense of distance—not only the distance of roads, mountains, fields, or horizons, but the deeper distance between the person who remembers and the person who once lived through what is remembered.

In this way, the boundary between inner and outer worlds begins to blur. The landscape seems to think; the mind seems to become a landscape. A frozen river may suggest emotional paralysis. A barren plain may suggest loneliness. A distant mountain may stand for some inaccessible truth within the self. The text does not explain these correspondences directly, but allows them to gather force through repetition and atmosphere. The reader is invited to feel that the visible world and the invisible life of the mind are not separate realms, but two forms of the same mystery.

The journey described, then, is not merely geographical. It is an inward passage through memory, estrangement, and self-recognition. The most remote country is not found beyond the horizon but within the speaker’s own consciousness. To travel there is difficult because it requires confronting what has been forgotten, distorted, or avoided. The self becomes a vast and uncertain terrain, full of dark woods, blank spaces, sudden openings, and dangerous silences.

By presenting inner reckoning as a kind of expedition, the text gives emotional life the scale of myth or wilderness. The struggle to understand oneself becomes as immense as crossing a desert or climbing a mountain. The stark, surreal imagery suggests that this journey cannot be mapped in ordinary language. It must be approached indirectly, through symbols, fragments, and haunting natural scenes. In the end, the text suggests that the farthest distance is not between one place and another, but between the self we inhabit and the self we have yet to understand.
outputs.L5:
The ice lay thick across the empty field, shining like glass beneath the pale morning sky. Along the fence, a row of crows watched in silence, their black feathers sharp against the white frost. One of them hopped down beside a crushed tin can half-buried in the snow and tapped it with its beak, making a small metallic sound that echoed in the cold air.

For a moment, nothing moved except the crows and the drifting mist. Then the wind rolled the can across the ice, and the birds lifted into the sky, calling loudly as if they had discovered some secret hidden in winter.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented prose poem in a surreal, wintry landscape, using images of ice, crows, sand, shadows, and inner/outer worlds, with a meditative tone about memory and selfhood.
counterfactuals.output:
At the edge of the white field, I found my shadow waiting.

It had grown thin in the cold.  
A ribbon of ash.  
A black root beneath the ice.

Above us, crows turned in the sky like burnt thoughts, each wingbeat loosening a little snow from the clouds. Their cries did not fall downward. They moved inward, entering the chest, striking the old rooms where memory keeps its bowls of sand.

I walked.

The world was wintered over: trees sealed in glass, fences half-erased, the river pretending not to move. Beneath the ice, something dark rehearsed its own name. I bent close and listened.

It sounded like myself before language.

It sounded like a door being covered by snow.

There was sand everywhere, though no sea was near. It gathered in the hems of my coat, in my mouth, in the folds of my gloves. Pale grains, cold as stars. I thought of deserts hidden inside snowfields, of summers buried in the bodies of stones. I thought of the child I had been, kneeling in a bright yard, building a house that the wind entered easily.

The crows descended.

They stood around me in a circle, solemn as monks, their eyes holding the outer world: field, sky, ice, my body upright and breathing. But inside their black feathers was another weather. A smaller night. A corridor of mirrors. I saw myself there—many selves—walking away from one another.

One carried a lantern.

One carried a bowl of frozen water.

One carried nothing and was happiest.

Memory is not a country, I whispered. It is weather passing through a country. It leaves frost on the bedsheets, feathers in the sink, sand at the threshold. It rearranges the furniture while we sleep. In the morning we say: this is my room, this is my face, this is the life I remember.

But the walls are breathing.

But the mirror is full of snow.

My shadow touched the ice and became a road. I followed it into the blue hush where the inner world and outer world leaned toward each other, almost touching, like two animals drinking from the same hole in the frozen river.

There, under the transparent skin of winter, I saw everything I had lost.

Not gone.

Changed into water.

Changed into crow-flight.

Changed into the silence between one footstep and the next.

I knelt and pressed my palm to the ice. From below, another palm rose to meet it—mine, perhaps, or the self I had forgotten in order to continue. Between us: cold, clear distance. Between us: the whole shining weight of being alive.

The crows lifted.

My shadow entered me again.

And the snow began, grain by grain, to remember the sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental lyric poem in short sections separated by bullets, exploring distance, travel, the past, and the idea that “nothing is as far as here.”
counterfactuals.output:
•  

The map folds its blue bones inward.  
Every road becomes a crease  
where a hand once pressed, deciding.

I have been leaving for years  
without arriving anywhere  
but more deeply in the room.

•  

Train window: a moving mirror.  
My face laid over fields,  
over cows, over stations  
with names like forgotten relatives.

The past keeps pace beside me,  
not behind—  
a dark horse in the glass.

•  

I carried a country in my mouth  
until language tasted of weather.

At the border, they asked  
what I had to declare.

I said: distance.  
I said: the orchard where no one waits.  
I said: a suitcase full of nearly.

•  

Airports are churches  
for the religion of elsewhere.

We kneel to our luggage.  
We confess to machines.  
We ascend through fluorescent gates  
into the white unanswering.

Still, when the plane lifts,  
the heart stays heavy,  
a town seen from above  
and never entered.

•  

Once, you wrote my name  
on a postcard from the coast.

The sea behind your words  
has not stopped moving.

I keep it in a drawer  
with other small failures:  
a ticket stub, a dead key,  
the photograph where we are smiling  
because we do not know yet.

•  

What is farther—  
the moon in its cold window,  
or the kitchen  
where my mother hummed  
over boiling water?

What is farther—  
the city I crossed an ocean to reach,  
or the afternoon  
I became old enough  
to lie?

•  

The road says go.  
The body says remember.  
The horizon keeps removing  
its bright mask.

I have stood in deserts  
where silence had teeth.  
I have slept in rooms  
that forgot me by morning.

And still:  
nothing is as far as here.

•  

Here:  
the cup with its chipped rim.  
Here:  
rain rehearsing the roof.  
Here:  
my hands, two travelers  
returning empty.

The past is not a place  
but a weather system.

It enters.  
It sits down.  
It wears your coat.

•  

If I could send a letter  
to the person I was,  
I would address it:

To the one already gone,  
care of the one who remains.

Inside, only a blank page—  
a white field,  
a snowfall,  
a road before footsteps.

•  

Night arrives without luggage.

Stars loosen their pins  
from the black map.

Somewhere, a train  
continues without me.  
Somewhere, the sea  
keeps practicing distance.

I close my eyes  
and travel the smallest road:  
from breath  
to breath,  
from then  
to now,  
from here  
to here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary poetic passage that sounds like translated Eastern European modernism: bleak, philosophical, image-heavy, and elliptical, with lines about seasons, mountains inside the body, and discarded selves.
counterfactuals.output:
In the fourth season, which is not winter,  
the fields turn their pockets inside out  
and find only ash, a button, a blackened seed.

I carried the mountain under my ribs for years.  
Its goats ate the little grass of my sleep.  
Its snowmelt entered my speech  
and made every word limp toward the sea.

No one returns whole from the marketplace of mirrors.  
We leave ourselves there—  
one self in a cracked bowl,  
one folded into a soldier’s boot,  
one hanging like damp linen  
behind the house of the dead.

Spring arrived without conviction.  
A few green arguments rose from the mud,  
then lowered their heads.

What is a life but weather rehearsing a face?  
What is the soul but a corridor  
where footsteps continue  
after the walker has vanished?

At dusk the city counted its windows  
and came up short.  
The moon, that bureaucrat of ruins,  
stamped silver on the abandoned factories,  
on the dogs sleeping in doorways,  
on our old names  
piled beside the road.

Inside me the mountain shifted.  
An avalanche of unsaid things  
buried the village of my heart.  
Only the church bell remained above snow,  
ringing for no doctrine,  
for no rescue,  
only ringing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dreamlike sequence of aphoristic prose-poem fragments about time, identity, and place, ending by repeating a striking sentence from the beginning.
counterfactuals.output:
The clock had a shadow, and the shadow was older than the clock.

I woke in a city that remembered me incorrectly. Its streets called me by names I had shed in childhood, names with milk teeth, names that limped behind me like small loyal animals.

Time did not pass there. It gathered.

In the square, an old woman sold maps of places that had not yet forgiven their travelers. I bought one of my own face and folded it until it became a door.

Every house is a question the body answers by entering.

I found my father’s laugh under a bridge, still warm, still skipping over stones. I carried it in my mouth all day and spoke with his weather.

At noon, the bells rang inward. Birds fell upward into the blue handwriting of the sky.

I asked a window who I was. It showed me a room I had never lived in, where a child was arranging my future griefs in a drawer.

Place is the memory of standing still.

By evening, the river had changed its mind and flowed through the train station. Passengers boarded reflections. Departures arrived wearing wet shoes.

There are years that live outside the calendar, grazing in the dark.

I met myself at a café near the border of sleep. One of us was late. One of us had always been waiting. We drank coffee from cups shaped like small moons and did not discuss the war between our names.

A passport is only a wound with official language.

Night opened its black umbrella. Beneath it, the town became intimate with its ghosts. Lamps burned like thoughts no one dared to finish.

I kept walking until the road forgot its purpose.

At the edge of the fields, a sign read: YOU ARE HERE. But the arrow pointed to the sky, where my first home floated, lit from within by people I had been.

Time is a room that rearranges itself while we sleep.

I lay down in the grass and heard the earth practicing my footsteps. Somewhere, tomorrow was putting on my coat. Somewhere, yesterday was learning to close the door gently.

When I woke, the city was gone. Only its dust remained on my tongue, tasting of rain, iron, and a name I almost recognized.

The clock had a shadow, and the shadow was older than the clock.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an original poem in the style of stark surrealist notebook fragments, mixing natural imagery with abstract reflections on memory, interiority, and the difficulty of simple words.
counterfactuals.output:
In the field, a white horse  
forgot the shape of grass.

I wrote this down  
and the sentence closed like an eye.

Morning:  
a bowl of water  
holding the sky’s unfinished face.

I said *home*  
and the word became a room  
with no door,  
only a chair listening.

Birds crossed the winter pane.  
Not flying—  
being erased in a practiced manner.

Memory is not a road.  
It is the stone you carry  
until your hand believes  
it was born around it.

At noon, the trees stood in their dark coats,  
speaking root-language  
to the dead.

I wanted a simple word.  
Bread.  
Rain.  
Mother.

Each one opened  
and showed its machinery:  
rust, feathers, a little blood,  
the dim stairwell under childhood.

Inside me, someone keeps a notebook  
underwater.

The ink moves away  
from every confession.

There are days  
when the heart is a locked orchard  
and the fruit falls upward  
into a sky no one can eat.

I touch the window.  
It touches back  
with the cold patience of glass.

Outside, the moon lies down  
in a ditch of milk.

I try again:

*Light.*

But even light  
has a shadow  
where it remembers being fire.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
